comments.author: Gowtham SB
comments.comment: The Agent Evaluation course is probably the highest ROI one here. Most teams can build a demo agent in a week, but the hard part is defining pass/fail criteria, regression tests, and trace-level debugging before users touch it.

comments.author: Amit Kumar
comments.comment:
A judge with high repeatability is still just a deterministic source of bias unless you calibrate it against task-level ground truth.

For agents, I’ve found the useful split is: deterministic checks for invariants, retrieval grounding, tool args, and schema validity - then LLM judges only for the parts that are genuinely semantic.

What’s your take on where the boundary should sit between deterministic evals and model-graded evals?

comments.author: Thomas Veit
comments.comment: The hard part is not adding tools, it is deciding what the agent is allowed to forget. I’ve seen memory quality matter more than model quality once the workflow becomes daily infrastructure. What rules are you using for pruning or aging out old context?

comments.author: Gustavo Catalano
comments.comment: Persistence without a good state model turns into expensive retry loops. The real jump happens when the agent can track hypotheses, failed paths, tool outputs, and constraints in a way that survives across attempts. How are you deciding what gets written into memory versus left in the current context?
